newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European Union launches year against racism.
newsitem.headline: European Union launches year against racism.

text.p: The European Year against Racism was officially declared open on Thursday as the EU vowed to fight racial discrimination, xenophobia and anti-Semitism, which it says pose a major challenge to society.
In a declaration signed at the start of a two-day launch, the Union affirmed its opposition to discrimination and its commitment to step up the fight against racism.

"After many years of ground work, this year marks the first time that Community institutions and member states have entered into partnership to take concrete action to combat racism," European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said.

"Racism remains an ugly reality in all our societies. Across Europe individuals are scarred by the wounds of bigotry...and the underlying current of discrimination that is an all too familiar picture in Europe today."

The Year, which has a budget of 4.7 million European currency units ($5.55 million), aims to support the efforts of organisations working to combat racism and to promote effective strategies by helping anti-racist groups exchange information.
It will monitor racist incidents, racism in policing, education and public administration and discrimination in the workplace -- unions and employer organisations will be involved.
The message will also be aimed at the grass-roots level, trying to raise awareness through media, culture and sport.
In the kick-off to the sporting component of the year on Wednesday an African all-star soccer team beat a European selection in Lisbon.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok stressed that national administrations, above all, would be expected to set an example to the rest of society in efforts against racial discrimination.
"Governments, together with interest groups, will have to do everything in their power to fight prejudice and encourage tolerance and forebearance," he said.

Kok said the Netherlands' would do all it could to gain agreement on the establishment of a European monitoring centre for racism and xenophobia before the end of the Dutch presidency. Britain denied on Monday reports that it had vetoed plans to set up the centre.

A European Commission proposal calls for the centre to supply EU institutions and national governments with objective data on racism, xenophobia and anti-Semitism and to set up a European Racism and Xenophobia Information Network.
Commission president Jaques Santer also expressed hopes of a speedy genesis for the monitoring centre and said racism was a prime area for cooperation between member states.
"Racism has an obvious European dimension -- no member state is immune to it," he said.
